utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. There are a few procedural matters to be discussed but the Chamber would prefer to do that after the first break. That means that I'll first remind you, Mr. Krajisnik, that you are still bound by the solemn declaration. I think you can repeat my words by heart by now but it's my duty to remind you. Mr. Stewart, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we were looking yesterday evening at the very end of the 10th session of the Serb Assembly. That was page 50 in the English, page 77. Do you see that, Mr. Krajisnik? It's the conclusions. It's where there was a -- first of all a rejection of the European Community documents.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the session of the 11th of March, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is, yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And the page is 50 -- no, 77 -- no, 77 in our version, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Remind us, we did read this. You made the following proposals and it was to authorise the representatives to continue negotiations with the other two ethnic communities in the presence of the European Community. And then, subject to the following restrictions and the minimum below which the negotiators must not go in representing the interests of the Serbian people, are the results of the plebiscite or a confederal setup of Bosnia-Herzegovina which entails three sovereign national states which may be linked up on the confederal principle. Mr. Krajisnik, that wasn't what you wanted, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. President, you said that there was a mistake here. First of all, on our agenda, according to our agenda we were supposed to state our views on the European Union whereas here I am presenting the conclusions of the working group which had been established earlier on, as mentioned on the previous page. This is a working group that provided an alternative, so that everything would not be rejected. That is to say the proposal of the European Union. That is why I presented this on behalf of the working group. Actually, the vice-president who was chairing the session asked me to do that. So the Presiding Judge was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: You've lost me, Mr. Krajisnik. I'm more interested in simply your answer to my question than the reminder that His Honour was correct previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I think -- one of the last things I said yesterday to Mr. Krajisnik, please think it over, overnight, and he now, in order not to forget it, I take it, you revisit the matter, which has been done now. So perhaps the next you do is to answer the question now of Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered your question. Perhaps implicitly. What I presented here was not my own proposal but the proposal of the working group. I was neutral. Because these conclusions, in a way, gave the negotiations a chance to be continued, and that was my objective. My objective was not to have them rejected but to have them continued. If I may say, I favoured such conclusions but these were the proposals of the working group. I do beg your pardon for answering the Presiding Judge as well, but I just wanted to say that this was the proposal of the working group which I presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, the questions come from me, the answers really are for Their Honours. Let's break it down. There are two elements there. The first one, as you've made clear, authorisation to continue the negotiations. That plainly was what you wanted. That's clear, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: But the second limb, the restriction, the minimum below which the negotiators must not go, so you were on the face of this to be tied by the Assembly decision here, adopting those proposals, you were to be tied to the results of the plebiscite or a confederal setup of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which entailed three sovereign national states, you -- you, the negotiating team, didn't want that restriction, did you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But these were the conclusions from the previous session so this working group built this into it. No, we didn't want that, but I already mentioned what the working group proposed. The first conclusion was the most important one for me, that we should continue the negotiations. As for the rest, we didn't really want that because our possibilities were highly restricted. There was very little manoeuvring space for negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then if we go over the -- we can see that that was -- that proposal you put with the restriction was unanimously adopted, and then if we go over the page to 51 of the English, it's probably 78, the next page, could even be 79 in your version, we see under heading of a contribution by you, "Please take note of the fact that the authorised persons are ..." and then you list them: "Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, Buha, Maksimovic, and myself, said Mr. Krajisnik." So in the end that proposal was adopted and the negotiating team, as authorised, from then on consisted of the six of you, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was confirmed that which had already been passed as an Assembly decision previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we turn back, then, Mr. Krajisnik, to page 54 of this document in your version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's page 36 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Rakic speaking. And more or less against number 14 in the margin, there is a paragraph beginning, "On the basis of everything we have gone through ..." Do you see that? Just above the number 14.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I see here is I propose that we take our territories, and where is this section you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's the immediately preceding paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I see. It's different here. Yes, "From the elections until this day ..." that's probably what you're referring to, that's that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It is indeed. "On the basis of everything we have gone through since the elections to date, we Serbian deputies have reached the conclusion that we simply must not agree to a solution different from that expressed at the plebiscite or, at worst, our own state of BH. Everything else poses a danger to peace. It has already been endangered, and the only alternative is not to allow the formation of Independent State of Croatia in these territories. "I propose that we occupy our territories and keep them, and not surrender them to anyone." Did you understand Mr. Rakic to be talking about territories which were in dispute or in conflict with Croats or more widely about Serb territories throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand what he was saying at all. And I wasn't paying any attention to what he was saying because it was not important. I can interpret this, if you wish, what he meant by this, because I know where he's from and I know what his meaning was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In referring to occupation of territories, was he at that -- proposing action on the ground to take over territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, no. What he thought was that we should now take our territories in the sense of introduce our government in our territories and not let anyone in. It's this regionalisation that was already referred to, that we should safeguard this and not let anyone in. That is totally unrealistic and that's why I didn't pay any attention to this, because we are talking about a solution for all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, not about a unilateral move, that we won't let our own go and the rest should be in accordance with the agreement. This was no war option. He means we are going to keep our own territories and we won't let anyone in, because what is being discussed here is a political solution all the time. There was no mention of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The next speaker, and that's page 37 of the English, and it will be, I think, probably page 56 on yours, but Professor Vojislav Maksimovic speaks. Do you see the heading where he begins? It's immediately after Mr. Rakic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And let's go to -- it's marked 15A in the margin of your version. That's page 57. It's right in the middle of page 38 of the English. And he says, "From this place --" We have just seen a moment ago that Mr. Maksimovic is one of the people who is to be a member of the negotiating team as approved by this Assembly. Here he says: "We are fully aware of the discord in Serbia and Montenegro and will not --" So sorry, I meant to start the previous paragraph. "From this place let us also send a message to our brethren in Serbia and Montenegro to wake up in the face of danger, and warn them that if they adopt a passive stance, a vast part of the Serbian nation, perhaps the most select part - our people in Bosnia and Herzegovina - will be cut off from the whole of our national being. "We are fully aware of the discord in Serbia and Montenegro and will not add to it. But, we Serbs in BH cannot wait for things to calm down nor bear too long their ruthless struggle for power. That is why we should refrain from taking sides in the Serbo-Montenegrin political confrontations. Instead, we should reproach them for their narrow and selfish views. We have not had words of encouragement or real support from Serbia and Montenegro for days now. It seems as --" as if, it must be -- "It seems as if the main political factors and figures in Serbia are silently watching our drama in BH. That is what our people are thinking, and they are waiting." First of all, Mr. Krajisnik, at this time, how well informed would -- was Mr. Maksimovic about the politics and the policies affecting the Bosnian Serbs and the Bosnian Serb leadership as compared with yourself?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Professor Maksimovic was president of the Deputies Club, a university professor, and a very influential MP. It is certain - at least that's what I think - that he knew everything the negotiating team knew. By his very nature, he's a bit temperamental and a bit radical, but at any rate he is a disciplined and reasonable person. At that time, he was not even a member of the Serb Democratic Party because he was the president of Prosvjeta. He is complaining about the lack of support from Serbia and Montenegro, and he is saying that before we kept hearing things from there to the effect that there would still be a Yugoslavia and now all of a sudden everybody is keeping silent so we have to rely upon our own resources only and find a solution. I would say that what you read out, up to that point, in terms of what he said, was realistic, positive, a bit temperamental, but you cannot say that he was not versed into what was going on. He chaired the club too, except for when Trifko Radic would take over for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can we go, then, Mr. Krajisnik, to page 73, which in the English is page 48.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Professor Unkovic speaking. Was Professor Unkovic an influential deputy?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mentioned Mr. Unkovic. He was not a deputy. I said that he was a candidate from our unit. He was candidate number 1 and I was number 2, and he was here as a guest from the municipality of Novi Grad.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'll put it a different way, then. Was he an influential person in the Assembly when he was present?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He was not influential. I mean, he could take part in the debate but he could not make any decisions. His discussion would probably differ from that what others had to say but he had no influence. Which is not to say that what he was saying wasn't similar to what some other deputies were saying, but he did not have any influence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: In the middle of page 48 of the English, it is six paragraphs -- well, it's five paragraphs down, I think: "I therefore --" Do you see a paragraph beginning, "I therefore kindly ask you, gentlemen deputies ..."? It's the fifth paragraph in Mr. Unkovic's contribution.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "I therefore kindly ask you, gentlemen deputies, members of the Presidency, Mr. Karadzic, to tell our army, the army in BH, the generals in BH: no more of either 'this' or 'that'. It must be either this or that. They finally must clearly state their stands." Was this position being adopted by Mr. Unkovic one to which a number of other deputies subscribed?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said several times that there were radical presentations, but that was a minority. A vast majority thought differently. Perhaps individuals had such a view, or, rather, not such a view, they were just saying that. I think that even Mr. Unkovic did not have this kind of view. Sometimes, quite simply, people are trying to come up with a version which is far more patriotic than others. Patriotic under quotation marks, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. You can put that particular document aside, please. And I want to go to the 11th session, which was held on the 18th of March, and that's to be found in two places: P65, binder 10, tab 109, or P529, binder 10, tab 388.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we are all working from the same English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, we see, first of all, it's page 5 of both your version and the English, Mr. Krajisnik, that an early topic of discussion here is Dr. Karadzic presenting the latest paper from the Cutileiro discussions, so he goes through that. I'm not going to dwell on that. He goes through that in some detail. If we then go on to contribution from you, which is at page 16 - and that's page 12 of the English, it's at the foot of page 12 in the English --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: -- there is a very short paragraph: "What is the problem?" This is you speaking, Mr. Krajisnik. "What is the problem? "I think the problem is that they want Bosnia and Herzegovina to be internationally recognised at any cost. They want it to be a state. "In this respect, it would be good if we could do one thing for strategic reasons: If we could start implementing what we have agreed upon, the ethnic division on the ground. That we start determining the territory, and once the territory is determined, it remains to be established in additional negotiations whose authorities are to function and in what way." Mr. Krajisnik, when you were saying there, "... it would be good if we could do one thing, start implementing what we've agreed upon ..." were you talking there about a unilateral action by the Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I've already explained this once but I can explain again. No. I was talking about agreement among the three sides. I was talking about the Sarajevo agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what I was asking you, Mr. Krajisnik. If we then go on, please, to page 24, which is page 18 in the English --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Srdja Srdic who is speaking and asks for the photocopies and so on, and then the third paragraph, it's the last paragraph, his contribution, he says: "I have had the chance to glance at some of the HDZ and SDA maps which Mr. Krajisnik has and which already contain the markings. I am a representative from Prijedor and I can tell you that the entire Prijedor area has been shaded as a municipality that belongs to the Muslims. Prijedor, however, is a municipality which definitely, even after the census and the elections, belongs to the Serbs. The reason why the municipality belongs to the Serbs is the fact that Serbs hold almost more than 70 per cent of the municipal territory, that is, of the land. I would therefore ask that all maps supplied and other materials be copied and distributed to all deputies. I do believe that our input in the way of corrections would help our negotiators." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, we can look at the maps, if necessary, but it was clear, wasn't it, that Prijedor was a municipality where there was a Muslim majority, taking the municipality as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You're right. According to that map of yours, the Muslim population had a very small advantage, looking at the municipality as a whole, the entire territory of the municipality, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. And then the map that you prefer, P293, the one that shows the smaller areas, inevitably that produces a more complicated picture, doesn't it, where there are significant bits of the municipality that are clearly Serb-majority areas. That's the position, isn't it? Just to remind ourselves of the figures, it was, according to the map P211, 44 -- it's a relative majority: It was 44 per cent Muslims, 42 per cent Serbs, and then 8 Yugoslavs and 6 Croats, so they are relatively minor in that municipality. But Mr. Srdja is talking -- Srdic, I beg his pardon, is talking about territory there, isn't he, Mr. Krajisnik, and what was the approach at this time of the negotiating team to the issue of municipalities where a substantial majority of the territory belonged to Serbs but there was nevertheless an overall majority lying with one of the other national groups?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the same approach, like Mr. Cutileiro. And this is what it was: We cannot view the municipality as a whole -- how should I put this? We should look at parts of the municipality, at the territory, and then on that territory, one settlement, if it belongs to one ethnic group, then it belongs to that ethnic group where there is a majority, relative or absolute, and in that municipality, a different ethnic group could have a majority in the settlement too and then it would belong to the different ethnic group. That is why I was saying that this map was the proposal underlying the maps. If you remember Mr. Cutileiro's map, near Prijedor, there is a part that is marked as the Croat part and the Muslim part, whereas Mr. Srdja is talking about the map that he saw, which was the Muslim proposal, where basically all of Prijedor was marked as Muslim. That is what their proposal had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I want to explore a particular distinction with you, and first of all make sure we got the distinction clear, and then ask you a question based on it. You can have a municipality -- and we see that with Prijedor -- you can have a municipality, say, where the Muslims are in the majority in that municipality. So on what you would regard as the more simple map, that gets coloured one colour as a Muslim municipality. On the more complicated map, where you break that municipality down into constituent units, you get a different picture, of course, because some of those - I apologise for the phrase - constituent units, which appears elsewhere, but the constituent units within that municipality, as we've seen and as you've explained, some of those will be majority Serb, some of those would be majority Muslim and, of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry. If I can offer a small suggestion. It seems to me that the use of "constituent units" is -- offers a characterisation that's -- invites some ambiguity later on. The map itself uses the term "settlements." It says so on the map. That might be the simplest way of identifying what we are talking about to make that clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm happy to make that change. I found I'd accidentally used the term "constituent units" and just continued with it, but I'm happy to switch to "settlements" if it helps in future.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So the settlements within the municipality, they may, of course, then be in some instances also majority Muslim, in some instances majority Serb, and so you can produce -- you can have a situation, can't you, where a municipality overall is, say, a Muslim majority, but the settlements, as they are shown on the more complicated map, where there is a Serb majority may constitute more than half of the total area of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're quite right. In one municipality, there can be a concentration of one national group in one territory bigger than in the rest of the territory in terms of the other national group. So in that case, the entire municipality belongs to that national group which is a majority there. We were discussing territories here, who was in which microterritory, so who was a majority in some microterritory, that territory belongs to them. A town, for example, is a true wealth, and villages will belong to others, to those who live there, whereas the town is going to belong to the majority that lives there. It's not the same quality. You've got forests and hills and mountains and also, on the other hand, you've got urban areas. So maps can be misleading when we are talking only about maps. We could look at the entire republic that way. So Muslims are a relative majority in the republic and then we can say that the entire republic belongs to the Muslims because there is the republic, there is municipalities, there is local communes, there is villages, so that was the organisation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, so we were looking at the lowest level group, that we base this division on the lowest level group, which was only logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, may I ask you, we have spent quite some time now - more than two minutes - on explaining something which is, I would say, so obvious. I mean, in any district system, you have ten municipalities, eight of the municipalities have a majority of 51 per cent, the two remaining municipalities have a majority of 100 per cent for the others, then you have eight votes gained in the eight majorities although the overall majority is of the different party. That's all really obvious.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I completely agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean, the English system of voting is different from the Dutch system, and you couldn't, with a -- which a minority could nevertheless gain the elections. That's for sure. That's -- depends on how the parties are spread over the different municipalities. So therefore, I think it has been hinted at already, well, five or ten times over the last couple of days. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, there is -- so we got that clear. Now, there is in principle, isn't there, another way of doing a map of a municipality, where you could colour in, in different colours, the land that was actually owned by different -- members of different ethnic groups.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, correct. Precisely. That is exactly what I meant. We were talking about land, not about a population. In one skyscraper you can have more people than in one entire neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, what I'm trying to do first is make sure we have a very clear distinction that there are three possibilities. There may be more in the world, but three that we are talking about. One is what might be labelled the crude simple method of simply colouring the municipality according to its basic majority. The next is the one that we did spend a few minutes considering just now, where it's broken down into settlements. But, Mr. Krajisnik, do you agree that what I have just put to you a moment ago, where you colour in the land according to the actual ownership of the land is different from that method, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. That's a third system but it's rather close to the second system we discussed, because the land that people live on is their land. I don't think the Prosecutor is right when he says that there is a lot of state-owned land. It's a fallacy placed by the Muslim side. On the contrary, there is very little state-owned land, only a couple of agricultural complexes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Stewart was asking about the systems first. If you take large units, then it could not properly reflect all the details on the map which might create a different colouring of the map. So therefore, the second system is you take the smaller unit and you get a different map. We've seen that. This map gives a different picture from this map. And then finally, if you would put on the map land ownership and the area of land owned by those persons, then both with an absolute minority over the whole and an absolute minority on all of the tiny little communities, et cetera, you nevertheless could have a majority ownership. These are the systems. Part of your answer was about facts, whether that was true or not, and you say the Prosecution was not right. I'd like to make a clear distinction between systems and how these systems would be filled in with facts. Please proceed, Mr. Stewart.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, where Mr. Srdic is speaking here and he says, the reason -- because let's be clear about this. If we apply what Mr. Srdic says to our maps here, basically what Mr. Srdic is saying could be regarded as saying the very simple map that shows Prijedor coloured for the Muslims is not the way it really is. That's one thing he's saying, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what he says, although he exaggerates the percentage a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then he says the reason why the municipality belongs to the Serbs is that Serbs hold almost more than 70 per cent of the municipal territory. That is of the land, he used the word "land." Do you understand Mr. Srdic to be saying that in terms of private ownership of land in Prijedor, the Serbs own more than -- whether he exaggerates the exact percentage, but the Serbs own substantially more than half the land in Prijedor and therefore Prijedor is a municipality that belongs to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how I understood him, but if I may add, in Prijedor the Muslims and Serbs made an agreement about a transformation of the Prijedor municipality into two municipalities. There were talks about that and they negotiated between themselves, so he is better informed than I am. They wanted to divide Prijedor into the Serb and Muslim municipalities. That's what he says. The same thing that was done in many municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's, for the purposes of my questions at the moment, Mr. Krajisnik, that's slightly another issue altogether. On the basis of what you have said, your understanding of Mr. Srdic's analysis here, was it the negotiating team's approach that a municipality where Serbs owned more than 70 -- more than 50 per cent of the land, effectively a municipality that belonged to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not a Serbian proposal. It was accepted as a model that all of Bosnia would be divided into the smallest possible units so as to identify territories where this or that side has a majority. For instance, down to a village. There is a correlation with property. But there may be people who reside in a certain populated area but own no land. Our approach was that the geographical and communication factor also has to play a part, because you cannot leave an enclave cut off if it is not contiguous to the territory of its mother constituent unit. So the ethnic factor could not be the only one. You had to apply some other factors too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Can you go to page 32, Mr. Krajisnik, which is page 23 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: This is Mr. Milovan Bjelosevic who is speaking, and he says, right against point 4C in the margin, he says secondly -- it's right in the middle of page 23 in the English. "Secondly, I would want to see more speed in the implementation of the law on internal affairs, I would want to see that things fall in their right place, and by that I mean things concerning the Ministry of the Interior and personnel decisions in the Ministry. I touched upon the subject two or three months ago, in the Assembly, but you, Mr. President, not only tried to stop me but prevent it altogether, saying that it should be accepted." Where he's talking about things concerning the Ministry of Interior and personnel decisions in the ministry, is he talking about the proposed or potential split in the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He's not talking about that, although from the first sentence you could think that he is. This entire comment relates to appointments in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and if you take it in reverse, if you take it inversely, he says, "None of this is functioning. You proposed candidates and you stood in my way," addressing Mr. Karadzic. We should transform and amend our law on the Interior. So he's complaining not about appointments in -- he is complaining about appointments in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in the Ministry of the Interior, and that was the main line of division, the cause of the rift. There were people in the SDA who stood in the way of any improvement and they were assisted by Mr. Zepinic who didn't implement any of the necessary changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we go on to page 53, which is page 37 in the English, we've got Mr. Vjestica speaking. And he says -- do you see point 5 in the margin? There is a paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: There is a paragraph immediately above that, which begins, "In addition to these two conditions ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "In addition to these two conditions, we must urgently establish a Serbian MUP in the Republic of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina, we must establish national defence, our Serbian army, which is already there on the ground, we just need to transform it into what we need to have. "In addition to this, we must urgently establish our own money transfers system. Following all this, we must take possession of all our Serbian territories, physically, with our own Territorial Defence, our Serbian police." Mr. Krajisnik, did you understand his proposal of taking possession of Serbian territories physically to mean exactly that, that he was suggesting that there should be action by presumably armed forces to take over territory?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm a bit handicapped because I read the interview given by Mr. Vjestica to the Office of the Prosecutor where he explained all of this. At that time, I didn't read anything much into his words because I know the man. He's very radical, temperamental. He talks more than he does, to put it that way. So I concentrated only on those of his proposals and points that were specific, concrete. He's saying here that he doesn't believe in Bosnia, but that's empty talk. But whenever you ask him, "And how do you intend to do that?" he doesn't know what to say. There are people who just find a valve, an outlet, in this kind of talk. I -- I read, as I said, his interview that he gave here at the Tribunal, and I know the way he explained this, and he did exactly what he said. He's a big man, not ill-intentioned. He talks too much, I would say, but there is no ill will behind it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we go on to page 63, Mr. Krajisnik, which is page 44 in the English, this is Dr. Karadzic speaking. And against 6B in the margin, he says: "According to the constitution and the laws there is a possibility for withdrawing all our men, from the MUP too. You will decide on when it is going to happen. "There is a law on SDA, and a decision has to be reached to activate it so that we would be able to formulate the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina budget. "It is good that we have created legal and political foundations for further actions, and it is upon you to decide when we will reveal our next move. It will all be happening in a flash and the setup of the de facto situation based on our documents. I think that the Council of Ministers will have to work around the clock to be able to prepare some additional laws, establish the SDK and so forth. We shall announce our withdrawal from MUP, not to mention that we have already obtained the badges. Our police will have to act in accordance with the law, no one must be harmed regardless of their religion, nation. Everyone must feel absolutely safe." Mr. Krajisnik, in talking about announcing "our withdrawal from MUP," whenever it might happen, was Dr. Karadzic referring to the same process that was in fact purported to be implemented by Mr. Mandic by the document that we have seen this week?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm very glad that you read this passage out. This position was very topical at the time. There is a decision about the withdrawal of Serb personnel. It was adopted on the 17th of April, 1992, whereby all personnel would withdraw - in fact, had withdrawn - except for the speaker of the Assembly. In other words, I did not walk out of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Mr. Karadzic here is saying what I said yesterday. The Assembly is the one to decide when that would happen. Why did they stress the Ministry of the Interior? Because the Ministry of the Interior was very topical, very important, and most of those who spoke at the session were unhappy about the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina and at the same time they saw that, according to the new arrangement, the police would belong to the Republika Srpska and they want the Serbian MUP to be established as soon as possible. He says this will be done, this will be done very soon, but this is a timed move. You cannot just go and set up your own MUP because you're unhappy with the present one without having reached an agreement about it. All we have for the time being are underlying principles. However, after this, the Assembly never endorsed -- never passed a decision for the separate MUP to be established, unlike what Mr. Mandic wrote. It was only on the 17th of April that the Serb personnel of the SDS party withdrew. It's all documented. The Assembly never took that decision. Which means that Mandic could not do this. And this is a good remark, actually, very well observed. The Assembly will decide. One person cannot take decisions of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then if we turn on to page 66, which is page 45 in the English, we see a contribution from you, Mr. Krajisnik, against the letter 6C in the margin. You say, just above that: "And since there were additional proposals, a schedule of our Assembly should be --" sorry, "a session of our Assembly should be scheduled for later because there is a whole series of laws that need to be prepared, and documents and proposals too, dealing with how to take over the de facto situation. "I have realised that responsible government should be established in Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. "- to find the mechanisms for implementing the BH constitution; "- urgently form MUP, national defence ..." Pausing there, Mr. Krajisnik, by your reference there to "urgently forming MUP, national defence," were you intending to say anything different from what Dr. Karadzic had been saying?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I chaired that session, and at that point, I was summing up all the proposals made by MPs, by various MPs. Each of those proposals was made by somebody. So I told them, "You proposed this." And there is a sentence where I say, "It's not my proposal. You suggested all these things. However, I suggest to you one conclusion." And that was later endorsed. What you read here are the proposals made by various MPs, and according to the rules of procedure, each proposal was to be put up for voting. But this was not consistent with our procedure, so I wanted to bridge this gap by making this summary and putting it up for a vote, the summary of these proposals, and I told them, all the draft laws and the proposed legislation, let's leave that for another time, for next time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And you referred then to money transfer systems and then "take the Serbian territories," and there again, Mr. Krajisnik, was what you were referring to there, "take the Serbian territories," did that -- was that meant to imply any physical action to occupy actual territory on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe this translation is not good. I was summing up what the MPs had said, without going into the meaning. You will find this wording, "take the Serbian territories," in the contribution of one of the MPs. Another MP referred to the money transfer system. The only thing that I said in my own name is the conclusion I suggested at the end. What I expressed here is not my own opinion or my own proposal. It's the summary of their proposals. On the contrary, if I had put this up for a vote, they should have replaced me then and there because it was not in conformity with the procedure. However, it was my duty under the rules of procedure to present this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik, perhaps I can tell you that whatever the Serbian says, the English phrase which appears here is certainly ambiguous as to whether it means physical occupation of ground, so I seek that clarification from you - yes or no - as to whether you had any such meaning of physical taking over of territory in mind there.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, it's not I who said that. I just repeated what the MPs had said, without commenting upon it. I don't care what he meant. You read a moment ago that it was Milosevic [as interpreted] who said it. I just said, "These are the things that you said. I for my part suggest to you to endorse only this." I didn't suggest that we pass the law on the MUP, the money transfer, et cetera. I just summed up what the MPs had said. That is the duty of the chairman, to summarise what the MPs had said and to put it up for a vote. I included even the contribution of this man Unkovic. If this is not properly translated or interpreted, and if I need to repeat it ten times, I will repeat it ten times, so long as you understand what this is all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the transcript, the name "Milosevic" appeared a few lines ago and the person concerned, we saw that earlier, is pretty clearly Mr. Bjelosevic.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Bjelosevic; MP from Derventa, now dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau would have a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Krajisnik is not saying, "I have realised [In English] that responsible government should be established in Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. - to find," et cetera, et cetera, but [Interpretation] you're not disputing this sentence [In English] "responsible government be established." [Interpretation] What you are not saying, you're not saying "I will summarise the proposals made by various deputies." You say, "I realised that the government, the responsible government, a responsible government, should be established in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina" in order to do such and such a thing. I realise that responsible government should be realised in order to do something. Is that the correct translation, or are you disputing this translation, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would appreciate it very much if you could read the paragraph before that. I could actually read it out, by your leave, because it ties in with what follows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Since there were additional proposals, a session of our Assembly should be scheduled for later because there is a whole series of laws that need to be prepared, and documents and proposals too, dealing with how to take over the de facto situation." And then follows this passage: "I have realised --" I have understood. Meaning on the basis of their proposals, I have understood that an accountable government and a responsible government should be established in Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina. If we look at it in isolation, then you can understand it the way you understood. But what I said before was that I understood, or I realised, meaning I understood what you want. And then I enumerated their proposals. That's the way it reads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, I imagine it is if one is looking both at the session transcript and the transcript today, but after Mr. Krajisnik read out the paragraph preceding the one to which Judge Hanoteau brought his attention, the -- Mr. Krajisnik then both read and commented upon simultaneously the next paragraph. Simply indicating that that is not a verbatim account of that particular paragraph. I know Mr. Krajisnik didn't intend -- I don't believe he intended to indicate that it was, but the record might otherwise be unclear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecutor is right, but please, this is very important. If there is any doubt about it, I would like it cleared up. This is not my proposal and I was neither for or against. I just summed it up. I don't know how it was translated. It could be ambiguous.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there is any translation issue left, Mr. Krajisnik, I suggest that, of course, since you are not in a position at this moment to discuss the matter with counsel, that the Defence will take the effort to specifically look on whether the original is translated here in the best possible way. I mean, we can't have anything more. You've explained what -- how you interpret these words, how you meant them. If there is any linguistical issue to be raised, certainly now the attention has been specifically drawn to it by you so that Mr. Stewart and Mr. Sladojevic and Mr. Josse know exactly what to do, that is to carefully review whether there could be any translation issue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm finished with this session now. And if it weren't inconvenient for Your Honours, although we are a few minutes earlier than the norm, it would be helpful, for practical reasons, to -- if the break were taken now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would suit us perfectly, since, Mr. Stewart, the Chamber also, for practical purposes, would like to have a break a little bit longer than usual. So we would have a break now and restart at ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As I said before the break, I'd like to deal with some procedural issues after the break. And I see that we received, during our first session -- yes. First, we deal with the, if I could say so, the double pension issue, the translation of the legislation. Mr. Josse, I read just now your e-mail that was sent today at half past 12. I do understand that translation causes some problems. That's number 1. That there was communication between you and the Prosecution, that you're trying to resolve the matter, but before entering into an agreement that you would also need to speak briefly about that with Mr. Krajisnik. One question: Would, not necessarily today, but would be a short meeting during a break just to discuss this matter, would that be sufficient?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It probably would, Your Honour. However, I need to meet with Mr. Harmon first of all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. No. Therefore I'm just talking in terms of future. So you would first meet and then, if there is any chance of reaching an agreement, then you would like to discuss it with Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And most probably a break, perhaps the first break of a day, a bit longer break would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I put on record briefly that I know the ODM heard my remarks yesterday. They have corresponded with me and a member of our team today and they really have been most helpful in trying to resolve this issue as speedily as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand. ODM, again?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Office of Document Management.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think they will appreciate that you put that on the record. So then we'll hear from you, I hope, soon. Could I expect that the Chamber will be informed not later than 10 days from now so that we are updated on how matters stand. Not necessarily that translations are already there, but just to be updated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Certainly. And come the moment that I actually need to speak to Mr. Krajisnik, I will apply to the Court again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One word at that moment will be good enough and we'll consider the matter prior to such a request to be made.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, yes, we have -- the Prosecution has submitted the exemplars of contracts in relation to housing. We have never set a time limit for any response. Mr. Josse, I don't know whether it's you or whether --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There will a response, that I can assure the Chamber and my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you're interested in know how much time you have got to respond. How much time would you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I was working on a seven-day basis. There will be a written filing from the Defence in relation to this rather large filing from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's, then -- things not always go as one wishes. Today is the 10th of May. Could we receive it by the 20th of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Could I say, I see Mr. Krajisnik is looking a little puzzled. It's worth remembering that of course he is not aware of any of these things the way that he normally would have been. No doubt in due course he will get this when it's been translated, but I just mention that in passing, that at the moment he is not aware of these type of developments until the filing has been translated into his language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As a matter of fact, I do not know whether we discussed the matter in his presence and whether it was at that time translated to him or not. But --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He is certainly aware that this is a live issue because it predates his going into the witness box.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And even now, of course, although he's a witness, we did not send out the witness, so the witness - but also the accused - can hear what we are discussing at this moment. So then, we'll receive your response in not later than 10 days from now on.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there would be any need, since you have no possibility to communicate, we perhaps -- if you're response arrives, we could briefly summarise in three, four, five lines, what you submitted so that -- it's not of direct relevance, I would think, for Mr. Krajisnik's own testimony, and if it's not, we could inform Mr. Krajisnik in this way that he's at least aware, without any further communication, what you did for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then Nielsen material. You asked for another day. Was that in order to orally argue the matter or to submit a written response?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We have submitted a filing in relation to this during the last break, and so the Chamber should receive that shortly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then that matter has been resolved as well. Then I would like to go into private session, or even closed session. I don't know there is anyone in the public gallery. It's reflecting very much, so I don't know whether it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm having difficulty telling, myself. There is quite a reflection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's what mirrors do, isn't it? Perhaps out of an abundance of caution, we would go in closed session. Perhaps that's the safest way of dealing with the matter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, please proceed. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. We did -- Mr. Sladojevic did have a look at that passage over the adjournment, Your Honour, and it's -- the passage is on the screen now, which was what we were looking at, "And since there were additional proposals ..." That paragraph and the next paragraph, "I have realised ..." Your Honour, it does appear to us that there is a translation issue here, so perhaps take it from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps we will do the same. If there is one specific translation issue, perhaps it could be briefly put on paper, given to the Registrar. Let's limit ourselves to what is really necessary, because the translators have a lot of work and therefore we limit it to the lines that are in issue. Unless you could explain it briefly in a way which could even result in agreement with the Prosecution. Of course, that's another way of doing it, if you just, in the next break, tell Mr. Tieger or Mr. Harmon what the issue is, they might consult their language assistants, and if the parties would agree on what the issue is, then tell the Chamber. That would even save further work for the interpreters -- for the translators.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's fine with us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I can say, Your Honour, it relates only to those first two lines before we get to the numbered -- the points with the dashes. So it's -- I have -- what we were looking at before in English: "I have realised that responsible government ..." It really relates only to those two lines, Your Honours, and we're as keen as --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you can resolve the matter, please do so in the next break. If not, then we'll send those two lines for review of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had left, then, that session, and we are going now to the 12th session. The exhibit numbered there, again there are two possibilities: P64, tab 266. Not sure which binder it's in, but it's tab 266. Alternatively, P529, binder 13 or folder 13, tab 443. And this is the 12th session of the Assembly of the Serbian People, 24th of March 1992. We got the version for Mr. Krajisnik in his own language, Your Honour, in the usual way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We have two sessions at that day. And this is the first, because I think both the 12th and the 13th session are on the 24th of March, just to avoid whatever confusion, so we are now talking about the 12th. By the way, you said tab 443, and that seems to be -- let me just have a look -- at least, in the list I have here, tab 443 is the 13th session, also on the 24th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please correct me when I'm wrong, but -- perhaps you could give the ERN numbers, Mr. Stewart, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we think it's binder 12, tab 266. It's possible, Your Honour, that I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you, in order to avoid whatever confusion, when we start, the first page you deal with, could you please give us the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. This is SA02 5781.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I do have a problem there. Let's be very alert on it and we'll find out immediately once you start quoting or reading. First part you'd like to draw our attention to, Mr. Stewart, would be which page in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's on page 16 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 16 of the English. The other one is supposed to be only 15 pages. That would resolve the matter. Yes the other one is only 16 --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. It seems to -- Your Honour, the ERN number seems to be the one that matches the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's consistent with our -- the ERN recited by Mr. Stewart and in fact in front of me at the -- at this moment in the B/C/S is indeed SA02 5781, but we have that as P64, P65, Treanor 11, tab 113. Also appears as P529, Hanson tab 389.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 389, yes, let me just have a look. Yes. I have the same sources and that's for the 12th session, 24th of March, although we still have some difficulties in having the ERN numbers, but let's proceed on the basis of what seems to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's also P64A, tab 266.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I've got that one in front of me, but I'll be alert on any translation issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think in the end the net result, Your Honour, is we've all got the same document, whatever its number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would be great.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think we have. Famous last words. Page 16, Your Honour, it's 27 of what you have, Mr. Krajisnik. This is Dr. Karadzic speaking, and he says, against the number 1 we have put in the margin, "I ask you now that following some instructions ..." Do you see that paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "I ask you now that following some instructions for national defence, information systems, et cetera that will be given here, the real and sovereign authority of the Serbian Assembly and Serbian people be established on the ground as soon as possible. As soon as we are informed that we have our own separate MUP, which will probably follow the coming session, all the newly-established municipalities should immediately set up police stations and all policemen should be withdrawn. Because this is, in fact, what life has taught us. Our policemen were forced out of the municipalities of Stari Grad, Gorazde and I think from Visegrad as well, et cetera. Policemen simply do not work together any more and this fact must simply be accepted even though it was forced upon us and tolerated so that supervision can be exercised." Mr. Krajisnik, are you -- do you know what instructions there Dr. Karadzic was talking about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Had you, since the previous Assembly session on the 18th of March, six days previously, had you been involved in any sort of discussions in which there had been any change in the leadership's position in relation to the MUP?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've said here what it was that I participated in, if that is what this is about. That did not happen during this period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could we go, then, to page 37, Mr. Krajisnik, which in the English is page 21. Dr. Karadzic again. He says: "Together with people who know these things we have studied what the establishment of the National Guard would imply at this moment. You can rest assured that the forming of the National Guard would also lead to the establishment of another two National Guards." Mr. Krajisnik, it's fairly clear, isn't it, that when he says "another two National Guards" he means that the Muslims and the Croats would also establish National Guards. You're nodding, Mr. Krajisnik. The tape --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Because that's in the agreement that we discussed, that is what was envisaged by the agreement. I mean with the European Community, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was -- did you understand Dr. Karadzic to be using that conclusion, that another two National Guards would be formed, as a point in favour of or against going ahead with the establishment of a Serb National Guard at that point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Against the establishment of a Serb National Guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: At this point in time, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then, if you go on to where you find number 4 in the margin, it's page 22 of the English, 38 of your version, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I've found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: The paragraph beginning, "You can be sure that numbers the police --" must be numbers of the police. "You can be sure that numbers of the police are quite sufficient. I know that the Serbs cannot do what the HOS is doing, to do things which are not based on law. We have a legal basis in the Law on Internal Affairs and we also have the insignia and at a desired moment, and this will be very soon, we can form whatever we want. There are reasons why this could happen in two or three days. Such are the forecasts but I cannot tell you the reasons now. At that moment, all the Serbian municipalities, both the old ones and the newly established ones, would literally assume control of the entire territory of the municipality concerned. The Zvornik municipality takes control over everything that constitutes the Serbian Municipality of Zvornik. Then, at a given moment, in the next three or four days, there will be a single method used and you will be able to apply it in the municipalities you represent, including both things that must be done as well as how to do them. How to separate the police force, take the resources that belong to the Serbian people and take command. The police must be under the control of the civilian authority, it must obey it, there is no discussion about that - that's the way it must be. I think we shall hear it today in the form of instructions at the Deputies' Club. "The decision must, therefore, be adopted but its effect must be delayed. It should not be at this moment for numerous reasons." Mr. Krajisnik, earlier in that passage, in the first couple of sentences, where Mr. Karadzic referred to the law on internal affairs, and then he said, "... at a desired moment, and this will be very soon, we can form whatever we want. There are reasons why this could happen in two or three days. Such are the forecasts but I cannot tell you the reasons now." Can you say what he was referring to in mentioning reasons which he was not able to divulge to the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened two or three days later was that the Muslim side publicly denounced the Lisbon Agreement. Mr. Karadzic is talking about the police here as an argument why we should not establish the National Guard, and he's saying that in two or three days, at the Assembly, they will receive instructions in terms of how they should act. We held that Assembly two or three days later, indeed, on the 27th of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then we can put this document aside, Mr. Krajisnik. There was another Assembly on the same day, the 13th session.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, this -- I give Your Honours the ERN number. SA02 5828 is what we have. And we have it, Your Honour, that that's found in P64A, tab 609. I hope that's the same one that everybody has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a reference to P65, tab 114, and P529, tab 443. Let's again hope that we are talking about the same document. At least the last document translation seemed to be literally the same, so therefore I take it that it is the same version of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Seems to be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I take it if the ERN numbers are the same, then they tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't find these ERN numbers on the copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I beg Your Honour's pardon. I didn't realise that Your Honour faced that practical difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So in this document, Mr. Krajisnik, at page 5 of -- on this point -- both the B/C/S and the English version, it's at the foot of page 5 of the English, Mr. Stanisic is speaking. "Mr. President, dear deputies and guests, I am Mica Stanisic. "You know very well my views and thoughts about the existing BH MUP Ministry of the Interior of Bosnia-Herzegovina. After all, I spoke up loud and clear at the press conference which we gave as Serbian officials about five or six days ago and which was organised by Mr. Velibor Ostojic, minister for information. "I do not think that the BH MUP is the MUP to perform the functions for which it was created. I said that publicly the other day." Mr. Krajisnik, we are seeing what we can do to get any published material or any documentary material relating to that press conference but not succeeded so far. Is that -- is that a press conference in which you participated?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I did not participate. These are Serb appointees in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Under the auspices of the minister for information, Mr. Velibor Ostojic, the government of the Bosnia-Herzegovina. So it is those cadres that had the press conference and presented the problems in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So it was a -- it was a, if you like, a separate press conference of Serbs only that were part of the MUP or the relevant ministries?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Serb cadres in the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was their press conference. And the minister of information was there, who was there by way of providing a service.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Were you consulted in any way in advance of that press conference as to whether it should be held and what form it should take?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. That press conference, there was no need for that, and no one consulted me about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: If we go to page 9 in your version, Mr. Krajisnik - this is page 8 in the English - you'll see a number 2 in the margin, and Mr. Vjestica is speaking.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He says, "I have not written any conclusion --" I'd better read the previous few lines. "The chairman --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Judge Hanoteau has not found it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So sorry. It's page 8 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but we don't have the same version, apparently. Because for us it's page 12, I believe. "[In English] I have not written any conclusion --"

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: That's what it says in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: It's page 12 in our version -- in my version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I only wanted to say that from what I've been able to tell so far, it appears to be a formatting difference rather than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see the numbers that appear on the top of the pages in our version are the L000, and then 1495, up to 1509, and that should correspond to SA02 5828, up to and including, I take it, 5840, and that corresponds with P529, tab 443, and P64A, tab 609.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's completely consistent with our information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So if it's just a matter of language, then it might be the layout rather than anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: It's entirely consistent with our information and understanding as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we only have to look at page numbers. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So immediately above where Mr. Vjestica speaks: "The chairman pointed out that the proceedings in the Assembly should be concluded with this item. "However, since a conclusion has been submitted for consideration by the Assembly, I would like to ask Mr. Miroslav Vjestica to read the text of the conclusion." Then Mr. Vjestica says: "Well, I've not written any conclusion. However, it appears from the debate which we've had here that the Assembly should adopt a conclusion instructing the Prime Minister of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the ministers to prepare, by Friday, an operational plan for assuming power, that is, for establishing power in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in particular in the field of internal affairs, national defence and payment transactions, so that afterwards we may together decide in the Assembly as of which date we are to establish full power and control of the Serbian territory in the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. This should be simultaneously effected in all municipalities where we already have a Serbian authorities and in those municipalities where we have only recently established Serbian municipalities." Very technically speaking, Mr. Krajisnik, there wasn't yet a Prime Minister, was there, but Mr. Djeric was about to become the Prime Minister in just a very few days, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the Prime Minister was elected at this session and he nominated two ministers. I think it's in the item of the agenda just before this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I think you may be right about that, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And he proposed Mr. Stanisic as a minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Krajisnik, and we get Mr. Djeric speaking at, it's page 9 of the English, it's point 3 in the margin in your version, which is page 10, and Mr. Djeric says: "The government will have the duty to draw up an operational plan and to submit it for adoption. We shall do our best to speed things up, to gain time wherever possible. There is no reason to think that we are running late in assuming power because a lot has been accomplished to date. Please do not take things in your own hands. You will receive your instructions and you will proceed as instructed." Mr. Krajisnik, was the task, then, of drawing up an operational plan, was it left in the hands of the government under Mr. Djeric, as indicated there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. That's how it was supposed to be done and that's how it was done, and it was the job of that small government that consisted only of three or four ministers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Then we can -- yes, we can leave this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, could we just ask for some additional information in this answer. When was it done and was it sent to the Assembly for adoption or approval in accordance with, I think it was Article 25, of the -- of the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. This was not proposed on the 27th, because that was -- that one was postponed. The next session was on the 27th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. There seems to be some misunderstanding. You were asked by Mr. Stewart, "... was the task, then, of drawing up an operational plan, was it left in the hands of the government under Mr. Djeric ..." And you said, "Exactly. That's how it was supposed to be done and that's how it was done ..." My question is: Was it then later on submitted to the Assembly for approval, as you earlier explained us would be needed? And where do we exactly find the plan as drawn by the small government?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I -- perhaps we are at cross-purposes. Your Honour specifically mentioned Article 25 a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, that I referred to 25 since earlier Mr. Krajisnik explained that in Article 25 the mechanism was described that plans should develop by the government and then put again to the Assembly for approval or adoption. That's the reason why I considered this, where it said government do so-and-so and then please come back to the Assembly, but perhaps too quickly I considered this to be what Mr. Krajisnik explained to us earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, my observation is only this, Your Honour: That the -- in the record of the proceedings here at page 8, or page 12 possibly, of Your Honour's English version, when Mr. Miroslav Vjestica is summarising the conclusion, the operational plan covered a wider range of issues than those to which only the -- to which the law on internal affairs related.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's forget about Article 25. Mr. Krajisnik said it was done as it was suggested here, government would draw a plan. And my question was: Where do we see that plan and was it then again submitted to the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know whether I made a slip of the tongue. I said yes, the government was tasked with preparing this programme, and it is normally its job. That's how it was done. I said normally the task was given to the government. It's not something that could have been done by an individual. I was talking about the task given to the government. I didn't say the plan was made and that it was submitted to the Assembly of the Serbian Republic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when your answer, I read that you said -- I repeat the question again. The question to you was: "Mr. Krajisnik, was the task, then, of drawing up an operational plan, was it left in the hands of the government under Mr. Djeric, as indicated there?" Your answer was: "Exactly. That's how it was supposed to be done and that's how it was done." So you meant to say by that that it was supposed to be left in the hands of the government and it was left in the hands of the government, but not an answer to my next question, as a matter of fact, whether that plan was ever adopted by the government and whether it was submitted to the Assembly. You said that's a different matter. Was that done finally or was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have the minutes of the 27th of March. As far as I remember, no such plan was presented. It is easily verifiable. We can look it up even here. I only gave the task to the government to prepare an operative programme, an operational programme. That was just a task. That was how it was supposed to be. And when I said, yes, that's how it was supposed to be done, I suppose -- I meant to say that it should have been the procedure, the proper procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You were talking about tasking the government, not about how this task was executed. It's clear now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right, correct. Maybe I was not too precise before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was just about to leave this 12th session. It may be worth, in light of Your Honour's observation, just noting that the -- that page, it's the last page in the English, whatever number it is, that: "The chairman suggested that the adoption -- suggested the adoption of a conclusion that the government should create a plan which should be timed carefully for operational reasons, and that as many proposals as possible should be considered by Friday -" which was the 27th of March, I note, and interject - "when the plan will be submitted to the Assembly. The rest can be done at a later stage." And then it was agreed there should be the next Assembly on Friday, the 27th. And Your Honour, we can go straight away, then, to that Assembly at the end of the same week. Your Honour, the ERN there is SA02 5841. And we have it at P64A, binder 14, tab 362; P65, binder 11, tab 115; or P529, binder 3, tab 72. I suppose you pays your money and you takes your choice for exhibits there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, two out of the three [indiscernible]. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, the first point is at page -- some hesitation, trepidation about page numbers -- page 12 of your copy, Mr. Krajisnik, page 9 -- sorry, you need the piece of paper first, beg your pardon. Your Honour, is it page 9 of the English? If it is, then I shall know we are probably going to be on the same page numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you start reading, then we can verify.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, yes. It's draft law, in the middle of page 9: "Chairman: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. "Let's now wrap up the first item on the agenda."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems not to be on the page 9, as far as we --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm quite sure, Your Honour, although it's a nuisance to Your Honours, I'm quite sure it's exactly what Mr. Tieger said, it's got reformatted and printed out in a different way. I'm sorry it's a nuisance to Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you have that at page 12 where you should have the number 1 in the margin.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think the reference by Mr. Stewart is at page 10 but it does immediately appear that the two translations are at least slightly different.
