I have the -- what brought me to this particular portion of the translation in front of me is the sentence, "The chairman thanks the speaker and gives the floor to Dr. Radovan Karadzic." It seems that Mr. Stewart has it in a slightly different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If Mr. Stewart reads, then we will follow the other version and see whether there are any differences which are --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Harmon is now bringing my attention to the top of page 13 of the English, which is more similar to what Mr. Stewart read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. If Mr. Stewart starts reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Yes. "Chairman: Thank you, Mr. Karadzic. "Let us now wrap up the first item on the agenda." And then -- well, I can go item number 2: "Draft Law on the Territories of the Serbian Municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. "- There were objections related to this law in preparing for this session, and if those proposing the law feel obliged to tender an explanation, I would ask them to do so. Then we would open a discussion of the law." And then we can go down a few lines to where Mr. Marinko Kontic speaks: "Mr. Chairman, gentlemen, my basic objection is that what has been put forward is a bill rather than a draft law. I think the law was drafted too quickly and is riddled with errors. One of those errors, for example, is that all the regions which should form part of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina have not been enumerated. For example, the region of the Kupres municipality has been completely left out. When I spoke with the gentleman who prepared this law, I was told that this was a result of no decision having been taken. As far as I can remember, at earlier Assemblies of the Serbian people, the decision was adopted that those municipalities which belong to regions represent constituent parts of Serbian Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you know that among the first 17 municipalities, Kupres became part of Bosnian Krajina. Consequently, according to this logic, it had to be incorporated in this law. "My proposal is that we discuss the law today as a draft since there are probably additional errors ..." And then you, a couple of paragraphs further on, said: "Is the proposal adopted that we shall discuss the draft today, with the proviso that we will have the opportunity to incorporate all objections by the next session and then present the bill and declare ourselves in favour or against it?" And the Assembly unanimously adopted the proposal. And then Mr. Rasula, just shortly afterwards, makes a similar objection in relation to Sanski Most. Mr. Krajisnik, so far as you can recall, these objections, points raised in relation to Kupres and Sanski Most, they turned out to be quite correct, these intervenors, in their pointing out of errors, did they not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only try to interpret. Sanski Most has more Muslims by one or 2 per cent. That's probably why the proponent of this law left Sanski Most out of this. The situation was similar in Kupres. I think the Serbs have a majority of 1 per cent over the Muslims. We adopted it as a draft, and anyone who had any objection was supposed to submit them to the proponent so that these objections could be incorporated as amendments, and can be incorporated in the next version, to be put before the next Assembly session that was going to vote on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we can see from the record of these Assembly meetings held with some frequency in March, the number of items and the number of issues that came up for discussion, and the number of documents. How well were your resources coping at that time with the generation of all this new material?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: On principle -- or rather, not on principle, but as a rule, every proponent was to give a rationale for their bill, to give background material to all the MPs to study, and then the MPs were supposed to voice their proposals. I, as an MP, also had this in my hand but I didn't have time to study it in order to express an opinion. I took the opinion of other MPs and the proponent as meritorious, so I refrained from debating this draft law because organisationally I just couldn't make it. I didn't have time. We didn't have commissions to discuss various bills. They were later established as bodies of the Assembly for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Could you turn on, Mr. Krajisnik, to page 31.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, it's, at risk, page 20 but maybe I'm the only one with page 20 in my version. But it's a long -- in this English version. It's a -- it's a contribution by Dr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Beginning at the bottom of page 22 of the English version we have in front of us, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik, you've got a number 3 in the margin and a paragraph beginning, "We know --" I'm sorry: "We have some indications --" I'm sorry, I'm going to go up a few paragraphs: "We have some indications that Mr. Izetbegovic has gone to Libya." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "We have some indications that Mr. Izetbegovic has gone to Libya for consultations with ... which finances various projects and which will perhaps attempt to ensure for him justification in Europe to walk out of the conference on Bosnia and Herzegovina. "We also know that they are looking for a cabinet for him over there and so forth. This means that we can count on their preparing for war in those -- in their words, they are attempting something." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, you were -- you were expecting to be holding, weren't you, a further meeting of the conference, the European Community conference, the Cutileiro talks, within a very few days after this Assembly session, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did go to that session in Brussels.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And at this point, the session in Brussels was on the 30th and 31st of March, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that was the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: At the point here, the 27th of March, so that's just a few -- that's a Friday, the 27th, I think, you, looking ahead to those resumed talks, what was -- I'm asking about you, Mr. Krajisnik, personally -- what was your expectation of what was going to happen at those resumed Cutileiro talks a few days later?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believed that by virtue of its authority, the European Community will succeed in forcing Mr. Izetbegovic and the Muslim side to abandon their decision that they had previously declared, namely that they were reneging on the agreement that we had reached in Sarajevo, and I expected that, instead, we would continue the negotiations and find a solution. Because prior to that, they had issued a statement saying that they were reneging on the agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then Dr. Karadzic carries on: "They can attempt to intimidate the Serbs here and there in Gorazde, they can kill someone in Brod, but they can never incorporate Serbian areas into their state or conquer them because they do not possess the forces required for the extensive territory held by the Serbs. "We know that our people have armed themselves. We don't know the various ways and means by which this was done, but we do know that the people have enough weapons." Mr. Krajisnik, by this time, the 27th of March, did you have available to the Bosnian Serb leadership, any sort of intelligence service?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were the existing services, the services that existed before, from the military, the MUP. I don't know all the services from which information and reports came, but I must say I rarely received information from them. I mostly received reports from my own associates. We didn't have a particular service, intelligence service, of our own.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: What -- what sources of information, then, were available to Dr. Karadzic as to the arming of "our people," by which we can probably safely assume he means Bosnian Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I suppose that he received such reports in contacts with the representatives of the SDS. I don't believe he had other sources. He received reports from the Serbian people. If he received any information, he couldn't have received it from anyone else. And that the people had weapons became obvious once the war broke out. All the three sides had weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, know that Bosnian Serbs had armed themselves?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to answer this. I didn't know in which way and how they were arming themselves. I just gave you an example as to how a resident of my village got a weapon. The army gave them 200 rifles and gave somebody else 800 rifles. I believe that most of them got weapons when they received call-up for mobilisation. As for things I heard second-hand, stories circulated that people were receiving weapons, and I heard some stories like that, like rumours, but nothing specific. I heard more about what the other sides were doing, that they were arming themselves. I heard more about them than I heard about the Serbs. I don't know whether it -- why.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic continues then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we receive clarification of the previous answer you have given, Mr. Krajisnik. You said, "I just gave you an example as to how a resident of my village got a weapon. The army gave them 200 rifles and gave somebody else 800 rifles." What army are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A witness was here, Krsman Sinisa, and he said that Zabrdje got, from the Yugoslav People's Army, from the Rajlovac garrison, 200 rifles, whereas another place got 800. I am talking about what was heard here, and I knew that that is what was done. I knew that Colonel Miletic did that. He testified here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Is it somebody else that causes concerns?

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Another place got 800. That -- well, we can check previous witness's evidence, Mr. Krajisnik, but what was that other place?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zabrdje, my village, and Sokolje, the Muslim village. That was the testimony of Mr. Sinisa Krsman, and that is what I knew too. Not in terms of these numbers but that is what happened, that they got weapons from the Rajlovac garrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, when talking about Mr. Karadzic, you said, "[In English]... received such reports in contacts with the representatives of the SDS. I don't believe he had other sources. He received reports from the Serbian people." [Interpretation] My question is as follows: You yourself never received these reports? Can you tell me that you were more cut off from the Serbian people or the representatives of the SDS than Mr. Karadzic? Is that what you are trying to tell us? Why was Mr. Karadzic better-informed than yourself, considering the position you held? At least, the way I see things, the way I understand things, you were not a simple member of an administration, you were not just any elected representative. You were a prominent personality. You were close to the people probably. So why, under these circumstances, was Mr. Karadzic well-informed about what -- about the people arming themselves, and why were you not informed of this? Can you please clarify that point for me. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know whether a word was missing but I'm saying that I assume that Mr. Karadzic received reports from representatives of the SDS, because that is logical, as far as I'm concerned. He was president of the SDS. If there was a party, and the SDS was a Serbian movement, he could have received reports from those who had armed themselves. I'm not trying to pardon myself now, that he knew about it and that I didn't. I'm just making a comment regarding his statement. I'm just saying how it was that he could have received this information. As for me, when the lawyer asked me, I heard some information from some people, but undefined. It's not that I'm saying now that I was not important and that Karadzic was important. Arming people was a secret. Perhaps people spoke about it only tete-a-tete. I spent more time in government agencies, whereas I assume - again I'm saying I assume - that he spent more time with representatives of municipalities, of local boards, and so on and so forth. So this is the grassroots, this is much bigger. I wanted to support this with an example from my own village. Had I known anything about this arming, I would have armed those people first of all. It was only when the war started that they got weapons from the Rajlovac garrison, because it was realistic that those who wanted to have weapons had to be members of the Yugoslav People's Army. What is referred to here are the people, I assume, although Mr. Karadzic says we don't have any paramilitary formations. But if somebody has some weapons at home, then - how should I put this? - it will be consolidated fast if there is a crisis. Well, that's what I managed to say by way of an answer. And then I added: Later I saw that people had lots of weapons, on all three sides. That is to say all of 1991 was involved in arming. How? That should probably be investigated. But that's my answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And when Mr. Karadzic said, "I must say, however, that we do not have paramilitary units," as at the 27th of March 1992, was that true?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I have no idea. Perhaps there were guards or whatever. I didn't pay any attention to this. But I assume that a maximal number of Serbs were in the Yugoslav People's Army. Paramilitary units were superfluous if you were in the Yugoslav People's Army. So my answer is, if I'm going to be honest, that I would believe this, because it's logical. However, when the war broke out, I saw some people who were armed but it wasn't that these were paramilitary units that had been formed - that's for sure - but these village guards or whatever. So I would support Mr. Karadzic in this, because that was his policy and his knowledge, and he kept saying, "Report and be on -- under the command of the Yugoslav People's Army. We don't want to establish a parallel army of our own." The policy was not to have any paramilitary units. Because paramilitary units only create problems. And you, on the other hand, have cooperation with and the support of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this the point where we take the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I had forgotten about the clock. We will adjourn -- have a break until 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Referring to a matter that was raised during closed session, I can inform the parties that Mr. Registrar has CD-ROMs available for the parties. Mr. Tieger, unless you would ask us to go into closed session, I take it that you have no responses yet to the questions earlier, or Mr. Harmon, so we'll wait. Could you please make clear to me whenever you have answers, that we turn into closed session. Yes. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, could I please have one of those CD-ROMs? If it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll discuss that with my colleagues. It is a bit of a different procedure, as a matter of fact. It's the -- I'll discuss it, whether or not. Mr. Stewart, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, we'll think about it as well too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there any need to -- if you would like to make any submissions in relation to that, we should do it in closed session. So whoever asks for closed session, we will hear the reasons at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we are looking at page 31 of the document in front of you, in your version. Dr. Karadzic is speaking and there is a paragraph that begins, "When you return to your municipalities ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "When you return to your municipalities, especially the newly-formed municipalities, I ask you to do what you are required and entitled to do under the law. The moment you arrive in your municipalities, you must urgently establish crisis staffs. You must try to organise the people so that they can defend themselves." Mr. Krajisnik, at this point, 27th of March, what was your -- and I mean you personally -- what was your belief as to the extent to which Crisis Staffs had been established already by Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any knowledge, but I certainly did not preclude the possibility of certain areas having established Crisis Staffs. As I've already explained, it is so easy to establish a Crisis Staff if there is a crisis in an area. Mr. Karadzic is talking here about a Crisis Staff in relation to what was previously said, namely in respect of the crisis and negotiations at the level of all of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which is something completely different.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And so he continues: "Find a number of reserve officers for those staffs and have them register everyone who owns weapons as well as units. They should organise territorial defence, and if the JNA is there, they must be placed under its command. If they are not, let them be placed under the command of reserve officers. They may not go anywhere but must remain in place to defend their territories. Half the numbers may be allocated exclusively for the defence of threatened regions." Mr. Krajisnik, before this Assembly session, had you been involved in any discussion with Mr. Karadzic about what he then said here to the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not participate. This is an improvisation presented by Mr. Karadzic, and it has a certain political weight; that is to say, to calm down the people who had taken part in the discussion previously. And to give them some instructions too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then the next paragraph, I won't pause on that, in Gorazde and so on. But then after that, a paragraph starting, "A war in Bosnia-Herzegovina will not solve anything." You see that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: "If it breaks out, you will get the plans. But I urge you to immediately organise the people within Territorial Defence units headed by reserve officers, form squads, platoons and crisis staffs and engage retired officers. This must be done throughout our areas." When Dr. Karadzic referred to the plans, were you -- did you have any knowledge of any, first of all, written plans already existing or in draft, such as Mr. Karadzic was referring to there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I mean, there weren't any plans and he didn't discuss any concrete plans. Mr. Djeric said something similar when he said don't do anything on your own, you will get instructions. That's a message. So that they should not think that a war would break out the following day. He's saying if a war breaks out, you will receive instructions, but there is time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then -- no, I can leave this document now. Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik. I've finished questions on this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honours, we can put that on one side.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it appears that there was a further session of the Assembly, the Serb Assembly, in early April. That would have been after the meeting in Brussels with Mr. Cutileiro, in pursuance of the European Community negotiations. How were things left at the end of the meeting in Brussels? I'll rephrase that. When you left Brussels at the end of that meeting at the end of March, how did you view the prospects for some resolution resulting from the Cutileiro talks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was still confident that we would find a solution, because in Brussels, Mr. Cutileiro had not concluded the conference. He said, "We will continue talks further." So irrespective of the Muslim side that had revoked its agreement on the Lisbon-Sarajevo agreement, there was optimism that a solution would be found before Bosnia and Herzegovina is proclaimed an independent state, because that was imperative. So I was an optimist, and that's the way everything looked, as far as I'm concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, a few days after those further talks at the end of March, there was apparently a further session of the Serb Assembly. At that Assembly meeting, was it the prevailing view among the deputies that you were effectively at war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this session that you're referring to, and the only one that I know of, is when the Serb Republic was proclaimed in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That was in Banja Luka. That was just a few hours before it was publicly stated that the European Community had recognised Bosnia-Herzegovina. I did not attend that session. That session was held in Banja Luka. There was just one item on the agenda, a political manifestation in response to what happened two or three hours later, perhaps a bit more than that. It was not a special session. We don't even have the minutes of that session. We don't even have stenographic notes. Just a declaration. I beg your pardon. These deputies in the western part of Republika Srpska, around Banja Luka, I think that they voted for two ministers, one for finance and the other one for defence. I don't know why. But there are no minutes and there are no stenographic notes from that session, and as far as I can remember, no notes were kept anyway. I don't think the second session was held at all. I mean any other session, rather. I can't remember but I don't think that one was held anyway. I mean apart from this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Why did you not attend the Assembly session you've just described in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put a question a while ago and I did not give you a direct answer, so let me say that by then the crisis had already culminated. Or to put it better, I saw everywhere that mobilisation had started, that this proclamation was being prepared, and there was a war psychosis in the making. Deputies could not travel to Sarajevo or from Sarajevo to Banja Luka. Quite simply, the situation was such that it was unsafe to travel around Bosnia-Herzegovina. We discussed it over the telephone and gave our agreement by telephone whereas they, in Banja Luka, had a quorum.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So who did you arrange it with in Banja Luka -- who was at the Banja Luka end arranging this Assembly meeting with you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the vice-president, Milovan Milanovic. I agreed, and in accordance with the rules of procedure, I gave my consent that he could have a session held there, because that is one of the rights of the president, that he can transfer his powers to the vice-president.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Was there any particular need to have an Assembly session at that point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was a need, because we felt betrayed. We were given a profound promise that these agreements would be brought to an end, that all of us together would have a referendum, that there would be a transformation of Bosnia, and that then we would change the constitution, and that Bosnia-Herzegovina would be recognised. The recognition of Bosnia-Herzegovina came without an agreement, without transformation, and it was completely opposite to what we had agreed upon at the very beginning, as stated in various documents and in Mr. Cutileiro's statement, when, on the 18th of March, we clearly reached an agreement and he made a statement that was recorded in the media. And that was the position of the European Community at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Between returning from Brussels and the time of the meeting, the Assembly session in Banja Luka that you weren't at, did you have any contact with the Muslim leadership in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And first of all, with whom did you have such contact?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Professor Muhamed Filipovic and the late Alija Izetbegovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Together or -- those two together or separately?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Separately. I had talks separately.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were -- was your contact with -- excuse me one second. Was your contact with each of those Muslim leaders a contact just you individually or did you contact them together with others of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had contact with Mr. Filipovic on my own. And I telephoned Mr. Izetbegovic and contacted him directly. I don't know whether there was anyone in my office but I did it myself, and there weren't any more of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Which -- which did you -- or who did you contact first; Mr. Filipovic or Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First I contacted Mr. Filipovic. I can explain both of these contacts to you, if you're interested. But Mr. Filipovic came to see me regarding this request to have an Assembly meeting held, and I have a book here where he notes everything down, what happened on that day, which is quite reliable.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, could you describe what you remember happened by way of your contact with Mr. Filipovic on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Filipovic is a renowned Muslim intellectual, an academician. He was president of the club of the Muslim Bosniak Organisation. They had two MPs. I had consideration for him because he was an elderly man and he had quite a reputation too. He could come and see me any day and any time to discuss any problem. One day he came to see me - this was after all the barricades and the crisis and everything - and we talked and he said that he was aware of the fact that there were problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let me just say one more thing: He was an advocate of that historic agreement between the Muslims and the Croats -- sorry, the Muslims and the Serbs, together with Mr. Adil Zulfikarpasic. Then he said it would be a good thing if an Assembly meeting were to be held so that we could discuss this problem. That was one of the subjects. And, of course, that the severed ties between the Serb and the Muslim side be re-established because obviously the most difficult problem was the one between these two ethnic communities. This was a rather lengthy conversation and then I suggested to him that he and I take action on this, that he ask Izetbegovic, that I ask Karadzic, and that we bring them together in order to see whether anything could be done in order to avert the obvious pending misfortune. Mr. Filipovic left, as far as I know, and a day or two or three later, I don't know, he informed me, saying, "I'm sorry I could not establish contact with Mr. Izetbegovic." So that was my contact. Because I wanted us to make a last-ditch attempt to avert a war, if at all possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And then your -- and then your contact with Mr. Izetbegovic, how exactly did that come about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the Presidency, without the Serb representatives, passed the decision to proclaim a mobilisation, and I must say that Mrs. Plavsic and late Mr. Koljevic were sent to run an errand so that they could not attend, and in their absence, they proclaimed a mobilisation. Then I called up Mr. Izetbegovic, and when he answered, I informed him of the way that they had adopted this decision, because it was an unconstitutional decision for the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina to make, and it was not appropriate to mobilise that population, the Muslims and Croats, because the institution that should have conducted the mobilisation was the JNA, which had Serbs in it. So this mobilisation that they proclaimed could only have been aimed against the Serbian people, and I asked him to do his best to cancel that decision because it was a dangerous one. I have to tell you the truth now. He told me, It's late, I can't do anything. And I felt when he said that that he wasn't quite happy about it. He wasn't glad that it happened, but the process had already started, and it wasn't going to bring anything good. So that conversation was a failure.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And did the conversation end with there being no arrangement or agreement for you and Mr. Izetbegovic to meet or discuss further?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was a day or maybe two before the war, before the armed conflict. Maybe it was even on the eve of the war. It was to be expected that I would turn up for work the next day, that we could try again to talk and agree on something, to see if we could do something. I couldn't dream that the next day would be a day when I wouldn't go to work, the day when there would be a, quote unquote, "peace gathering" that degenerated into chaos and set on fire the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So which was the first day that you didn't go to work?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's the 5th or maybe the 6th of April. I can't tell you exactly. It is a well-known date. I'm just afraid to get it wrong now. 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Of course, Mr. Krajisnik. Now, up until that day when you didn't go in to work, you were working in the same office in the Assembly building, were you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I worked in that office.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was Dr. Karadzic continuing to work in Sarajevo for at least for those first few days in April?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He worked also until the same day. Maybe he continued even for a day longer than I. He had a meeting at the Holiday Inn while that peace gathering, as they called it, took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: So Dr. Karadzic's office was still in the Holiday Inn, was it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to explain that. The headquarters of the Serbian Democratic Party was about a kilometre or a kilometre and a half away from the Assembly and the Holiday Inn Hotel. It was in Djuro Djakovic Street, the former seat of the Club of Deputies of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That's where the office of Mr. Karadzic was. There was a bauxite company that had offices in Holiday Inn that offered Mr. Karadzic the use of a room or some office space. So it wasn't his real office. It was just something that he used temporarily. I don't know whether it was one or two rooms, although I visited.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did Mr. Djeric, who, of course, had very recently become the Prime Minister of the Serb Republic, did Mr. Djeric have an office in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Djeric was a minister without portfolio in the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and he had an office in the building of the government, which was just across the street from the Assembly and the Holiday Inn. That was the only office he had. He did not have any other offices at the Prime Minister of the Serbian Republic. He continued on the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Ostojic, did he have an office in the same building as Mr. Djeric?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the same building.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And Mr. Maksimovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Maksimovic, as president of the club, who was otherwise working in the philosophy school of the university, had an office in the Club of Deputies to the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, just like all the other MPs.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: When you made the contacts that you've described with Mr. Filipovic and with Mr. Izetbegovic, did you seek the approval of Dr. Karadzic before initiating those contacts?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I thought the two of us should get in touch with party leaders. I believe that I did get in touch with Mr. Karadzic, although I cannot be certain now, but I assumed he would have nothing against meeting Mr. Izetbegovic because it was in the interest of our side to keep the contacts going in order to reach some sort of solution, and we didn't want the contacts and the negotiations to stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, we know that in April, 1992, the Bosnian Serb leadership moved to Pale. Who went first to Pale among the Bosnian Serb leaders?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who went first. All I know is that Karadzic and Koljevic went there from the Holiday Inn. I can't tell you all the people who went there, who moved there, because I spent that time in Zabrdje, at home. But even Mrs. Plavsic was not in the first group. She came later. And then gradually, more and more people called and went to Pale. I cannot tell you who went first. I just gave you the general picture as I know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, you said it wasn't Mrs. Plavsic, she wasn't in the first group, but you were not either in the first group, correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I wasn't either.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Did you -- did you eventually go to Pale without returning to work in your office in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I once went to Pale and then went to Zabrdje and then went to Pale again. I had a reason for that. And as far as I remember, between my first trip to Pale and my second one, I had that meeting at my office that you are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I hadn't just then talked about a meeting at your office, Mr. Krajisnik, but -- so identify which meeting -- oh, you're talking about the meeting with Mr. Filipovic, or some other meeting?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You asked me whether, before my departure for Pale, I was at my office. I told you that the 4th or the 5th or the 6th - I don't know any more - was my last day at my office, and then I went to Zabrdje. My meeting with Mr. Filipovic was before. And after that, the war started, so I didn't go to work any more. So all my activities, my meetings with Filipovic and Izetbegovic, my work at the office, all of that took place before the 4th.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, it was your answer, you said, as far as you remember, between your first trip to Pale and your second one, you had that meeting at your office that I, your counsel, was talking about. I actually don't see or recall from the record that I was talking about any such meeting. So perhaps you can identify the meeting that you were referring to there.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought we had finished with Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Filipovic, and that we had finished with my work at the office. The war started then. And then we discussed the matter of my going to Pale and when I went. I told you I went to Pale once, returned home, and then went to Pale again. And between those two trips, I was at my office, attending a meeting. That was already after the war started. I thought you meant to ask me whether I went back to my office again after that date. So this day that I'm now referring to could be the 15th of April or maybe later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Who was the meeting with?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stewart, I'm not quite sure. Is the meeting of any -- because it came up without you having asked about it, was it any specific meeting or was it just the last meeting you have in your office?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should have explained before. On the 15th of April, I was at Pale. That was after the war started. The 14th or the 15th. So I had went -- I had gone there and went back home. And then I went back to Pale again. And between the 15th and the second, there was this meeting at my office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was this any specific meeting or was it just one of many meetings and just being the last one? We are spending a lot of time on that meeting without even knowing whether it was just a meeting, or something special.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I meant the meeting that Mr. Kecmanovic explained about when I met with Mr. Izetbegovic during the war at my office. That's the only meeting we had after the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we are on track. What seems to have happened, Mr. Krajisnik, you -- Mr. Krajisnik correctly guessed that I was going to ask him about a meeting but didn't notice that I hadn't yet asked him. I think that's really what happened, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, yes, the meeting with Mr. -- with Mr. Izetbegovic, how did it -- I'm asking for your recollection and your evidence on this, Mr. Krajisnik. How did it come about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe it would be a good idea to put the map of Sarajevo on the screen so that you can see where Pale is, where Zabrdje is, where is the centre of the town. It would be useful because then it would be much easier to explain things, by your leave. I have a map here. I can give you one. Just for illustration.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: I'm not spurning your offer, Mr. Krajisnik. I'm just seeing whether we can find one that's conveniently already in evidence. The one which is in Exhibit 527, I think it is, isn't it, it's P527, at page 25, I wonder if that would be good enough for your purposes, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: We could use that one, then. Can that come up on the ELMO? Okay. So there we are, Mr. Krajisnik. We've got the Sarajevo map.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the strict centre of Sarajevo. That's downtown. The yellow area. This is Pale, and this is Zabrdje, here. And now, from Zabrdje I went to Ilidza. That's here. This line. There is a road there. Whereas Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Koljevic came from Pale. All of this is Serbian territory, was Serbian territory at the time. They came here, where the airfield was. And here, in Novo Sarajevo, in Lukavica, because there is Lukavica I'm showing now, roughly, from here, they crossed to the other side - this is Hrasnica, the Muslim area - and we had a meeting at Ilidza on the occasion of the arrival of Mr. Cutileiro. So they came across this territory and I came from the other side, from here.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: (redacted). I have never seen the man. I had never seen the man before. The only reason I went there was to see Mr. Cutileiro and Mr. Darwin, and I was with them during that meeting. There were two delegations attending from Sarajevo. They came by this road here. One delegation comprised Mr. Kecmanovic, and he told you who had been with him then. The other delegation consisted of Mr. Rasim Kadic, then president of the Liberal Party, or maybe the Youth Party, I don't remember what it was called, and Martin Raguz. We discussed how to stop the war that had already started. The idea of both delegations was to get the approval of Mr. Izetbegovic to meet here in the centre, downtown, near the Assembly building. I can't pinpoint it exactly, but roughly here. So I should have taken this road through Muslim territory to meet Mr. Izetbegovic at my office in the Assembly building. From that meeting, together with Mr. Tadic, who is a Muslim, and Mr. Raguz, who is a Croat, I went to my home, and I returned again with them. Mr. Kadic then went and organised a meeting with Mr. Izetbegovic in order for that meeting to take place between Izetbegovic, Kecmanovic, and myself. On that occasion, I took Mr. Kadic to my home, and his intention was to go to Breza, which is a municipality behind Ilijas. I asked some people who were there to do me a favour and provide him with escort. And they did. But he told me, he had received confirmation from Mr. Izetbegovic, that Mr. Izetbegovic was willing to meet me that evening at the Assembly building. And that evening, I got into the police car belonging to the police station of Ilidza with two escorts, went to the Assembly and met with Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Kecmanovic, and we met exactly as Witness Kecmanovic described during his evidence. There was a question that arose that I'm answering now as to how this meeting occurred in the first place. And then when I returned from the Assembly, I went to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And what time of day or night was it, then, when you met Mr. Izetbegovic with Mr. Kecmanovic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard a variety of versions. It was near dusk, so it could have been 5, 6 p.m., I'm not sure. But still, we talked long enough to be caught by the curfew and we were told that we had to leave as soon as possible because a curfew applied at that time. So we had that meeting at my office by night. It was dark. I don't know whether there were any lights available but they were not on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: How long did the meeting last altogether?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And were you, Mr. Izetbegovic and Mr. Kecmanovic present throughout?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The three of us were in one and the same room all the time, talking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: And was there anybody else present at any point?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Our escorts were left behind in the room occupied by the secretary. There was nobody else in that room with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm obviously moving to the content of the meeting, but I see the clock as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It might not be wise to start that at one minute to seven. We will adjourn for the day and will resume tomorrow, quarter past two, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 11th day of May, 2006, at 2.15 p.m.
